utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. Please be seated. May we please hear the case number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is case number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, Nicholas Koumjian, assisted by Ruth Karper, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Branko Lukic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. We have a long day before us with difficult exercises. We prepared ourselves long into the evening yesterday based on the presents given to us by the Defence. Let's follow the order of Rule 85. Doing so, we would start with the question whether or not evidence has to be ordered by the Trial Chamber. Is it necessary to go into closed session on the question that was discussed yesterday? I think it's appropriate. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then Rule 85(vi). Any relevant information that may assist the Trial Chamber in determining an appropriate sentence if the accused is found guilty on one or more of the charges in the indictment." We received the report requested by the Defence from Mr. McFadden, chief of the detention Unit. Any objections against the admission into evidence of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's not a lengthy one, but no objections, Your Honour, on our side.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then the next available Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: D128, admitted into evidence, D128A. It's my understanding, Mr. Lukic, that you can translate this to your client. Is there any other request for additional information under Rule 85(vi)? This is apparently not the case. We have already received a number of documents, especially character witnesses, under 92 bis statements by members of the family. I think we can be satisfied with this if need may be. Let's -- Mr. Koumjian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: There is one additional document that we had promised, which was to provide the Court with the sourcing of the Prosecution documents that have been admitted since the close of the Prosecution case, and we do have a list prepared by Mr. Inayat. We've entitled it "List 9," showing the source of those documents that came in from the Prosecution since the close of the Prosecution case in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you tender -- Mr. Usher, could you please be so kind and distribute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Apparently there were a few documents that were admitted, Ms. Karper reminds me, before the close of the Prosecution case but after the preparation of list 8, and they're also included on list 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think in the past we also gave these lists an exhibit number, so it would be only consequent. Any objections, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then this document would be S43 ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 7, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: S437A. Then before we come to this difficult exercise going through document by document, let us please continue in the order of Rule 85. Once again the question in the direction of the Defence, in Rule 85 para C it reads, "If the accused so desires, the accused may appear as a witness in his or her own defence." And under Rule 84 bis a statement of the accused would be possible. Is there any intention to do so under Rule 84 bis or under Rule 85(C)?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We don't have those intentions at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then let us try to find the appropriate date for the closing arguments. The parties had agreed in the past that the sequence foreseen in Rule 86 should be changed and therefore we should first of all hear the oral closing arguments and then also based on this and emanating from questions arising from these arguments, the final brief. We are a little bit ahead of our schedule. The rejoinder phase was scheduled until Friday this week. May I ask as to the fact that the Prosecution may present first a closing argument. First, do you want to present a closing argument and would you be ready to present this closing argument Friday, April the 4th?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No. We would like additional time, especially to make -- well, the make the argument as helpful to the Trial Chamber as possible. I don't think we'd be ready this Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What would be your realistic perspective?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, I think we're now scheduled for the following Friday. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: April, the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I think that's the earliest we could do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We discussed it yesterday, came to the conclusion this would be the latest possible, but then we would be in agreement, so let's envisage April, the 11th of April for the closing arguments of the Prosecution. Then it would follow that the Defence may make a closing argument. Is it your intention to make such a closing argument?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We -- our intention is to make closing arguments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you be prepared to present your closing arguments the following Monday; that would be the 14th of April?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we would be prepared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then let's fix it the 14th of April, 9.00. Is one day per party enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. But we would anticipate rebuttal to the Defence argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: All right. This would be the next step. You would need a day in between, or would you be prepared to respond immediately the next day; this would be the 15th?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, we could respond immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then may I ask the Defence: In return, you'll respond the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then what about the final brief? Previously it was envisaged to have this final brief ready April the 17th. But may I hear your point of view when it could be ready. Please first the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've asked some others that are working on that for their views. Obviously because of the Easter break, it's not really something we want to do, to have it after the Easter break, but we probably would obviously present a better product if it's -- if we have more time. I don't know what the Defence views are on that, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we first hear the Defence views on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that could be a joint motion for both parties. The Defence would like to have also additional time if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Easter -- Christian Easter here in the Netherlands, this would be Monday, the 21st of April. Would it be sufficient for both parties on the 28th of April, giving the opportunity to both parties to respond no later than the 2nd of May. If the parties so want, we could state that the final brief should arrive Monday, the 28th of April and any written submissions on legal issues would be taken into account when arriving no later than Friday, the 2nd of May, end of office hours; this would be 5.30. Would this be appropriate?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think we hope that we would give our complete legal submissions on the 28th, and I understand, obviously, the Defence is going to present a different view, but I don't think it will be necessary for us to rebut that. Our position will be complete on the 28th, unless the Trial Chamber had specific questions we could then re-address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: There should be a possibility that emanating from these briefs in fact there would be the need to discuss the one or other issue or that a party may want to respond. But it's only a possibility and it would be only taken into account everything what arrived -- what would arrive until May the 2nd. What is the view on this by the Defence, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that we can deal with this after the final briefs and that we can arrange with the Prosecution if it's necessary to have this possibility on the 2nd of May, because we think also that on the 28th of April we will have the final brief ready and final.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then the Trial Chamber, after having discussed briefly, hereby orders that the final brief arrives the 28th of April no later than 17.00 -- 17.30 in the afternoon, Monday, the 28th April. And then as mentioned before - and it's for the parties to discuss this - if need may be, additional remarks or responses on legal issues -- solely on legal issues would be taken into account for the judgment arriving Friday, the 2nd of May, no later than half past 5.00. I want, finally then, to give the hint that following the response given by the Defence, it would be the right of Dr. Stakic in person to give a final statement. The last word should always be for the accused. Therefore, if Dr. Stakic so wants, in agreement with counsel, then he has this opportunity, the 16th of April, immediately after the response given by the Defence. Anything else to be discussed before we come to this exercise of going through all the documents? This seems not to be the case. Then let's start. We have before us hopefully all, an entire set of lists, where we have the 65 ter number of the documents. The documents from 1 to 470 we have already the comments given by the Prosecution. We have not yet comments by the Defence. Can we agree that in those cases where the Office of the Prosecution had no objections, then without further adieu and without any comments given by the Defence and, in addition, we don't have any problems with the document, that this be then admitted into evidence but not immediately given a exhibit number, but I would kindly ask Madam Registrar to follow this exercise and give the exhibit numbers and then later to distribute a list of the then exhibit numbers based on the 65 ter number given by the Defence. Can we proceed this way? I can't see no objections. So let's start with 1 to 7 -- 1 to 6. This was already admitted into evidence. The Defence wanted to provide an English copy of the entire book numbered 2. What about this? Is it available? This would be the book "Who Defended Bosnia?"

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would it be too late if we provide this translation the next week, Your Honour? Because even my case manager abandoned me, so I couldn't find this morning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If there are no --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Prosecution can live with this? No objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then the OTP was kind enough to offer five chapters of book number 6. This would be the book "Tricky Strategy by Sefer Halilovic."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, they're available and will be distributed later today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I go through all the numbers, and please may the parties correct me if I am wrong. Number 7 was already admitted as SK8. Document 8 and 9 are admitted into evidence. Document number 10, you were missing a translation. We have only the text in B/C/S, apparently an article from Kozarski Vjesnik. One can't read it, 8 or 9 August 1991. I don't know which part shall be tendered, and therefore I can't ask in the moment whether this document is available in the archives or database of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we gave to the Defence -- or when they came to look at the newspaper, all translations of the ones they selected that we already have. So if Mr. Lukic doesn't have the translation, then we don't have it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To solve the problem, we can withdraw this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Document number 10, withdrawn. Document number 11, already admitted under the number D72; 12, already admitted SK21; 13, admitted into evidence; 14, admitted under SK22; 15, admitted into evidence. 16, may we hear the comments. There were objections by the Prosecution to this document, Kozarski Vjesnik of 13th of September, 1991, a newspaper article about a crime committed in the Zagreb area. We can't see any relevance for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, from this document it's obvious that the man is from Prijedor and is buried in the Pasinac cemetery in Prijedor. So although killed in Croatia, we think that it had some impact on the local commune, especially that -- because at that time there were no fightings in Prijedor area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Our general approach was and is that we would admit such kinds of documents on events happening outside Prijedor municipality; therefore, having may be an impact on that what happened in Prijedor, this would be admissible. But as to the fact that it's dated September 1992 -- 1991, we can't see the relevance and therefore not admitted into evidence. Document 17 is already admitted under SK9; 18, already admitted under SK9; the same is true for 20 -- for 19. 20 is already admitted under D83; 21, admitted into evidence; 22, already admitted under SK11; 23, already admitted under SK10; 24, already admitted under D84; 25, already admitted under D85. 26 is moot as to the fact that it's the same document as 25. Correct, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: 27, admitted into under; 28, admitted into evidence; 29, already admitted under D71B. 30, would you please comment on the relevance, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We can't object to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We know, but we took the liberty also to ask for the relevance of the documents. Mr. Lukic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This article only reflects as a general claim something that many witnesses testified in this case, that the 5th Partisan Brigade was in Slavonia in October 1991, so it's just as a background information. It doesn't touch the core issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Not admitted into evidence, we can't see the relevance for the concrete case. 31, admitted into evidence; 32, 33, admitted into evidence; 34, already admitted under D73; 35, 36, admitted into evidence; 37, already admitted under SK36; 38 through 40, admitted into evidence; 41, admitted into evidence. Then 42, we can't see the relevance. Mr. Lukic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I remember this one. It's also just a background data about the situation in the health institutions in Prijedor area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: November 1991, on drug abuse. The Trial Chamber held this was -- is not relevant for this case. Not admitted into evidence. Two other documents we would have the same problems, because it's a relatively long time before the events in Prijedor November 1991. Comments from your side?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The only thing that these documents show the situation in 1991 and the situation only deteriorated in the future, going closer to spring and summer 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Document 43, admitted into evidence. 44, saboteurs apprehended by Bosanski Novi police. What about the relevance, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This document shows that already in 1991 there were some terrorist actions in the region of Autonomous Region of Krajina. I think that this shows that even in 1992 the situation was pretty much chaotic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence; same is true for document 45. 46, there was an objection by the Prosecution to the relevance. We would share this view in principle. May I hear your comments, 28 November 1991, foreign currency black market in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is also back-up information about the situation in the Prijedor area. It doesn't touch the core issue. It only shows that legality was not observed at that time already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Here we agree with the view taken by the Prosecution; therefore, not admitted into evidence. 47, 48, admitted into evidence; 49, already admitted under D86; 50, already admitted under D87. 51, admitted into evidence; 52, we had some problems with the lower production of wheat because of bad weather, December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We think that this shows not bad weather but that many people were absent on the front lines and shortages in fuel distribution, so it does not touch the core issue but shows that even the shortages of food was expected next spring and summer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then admitted into evidence. This was document 52. 53, already admitted under D88; 54, admitted into evidence. 55, there was an objection to the relevance, and we would share this view. A murder of a Serb living in Croatia, document 55.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We mentioned many witnesses in -- not many but several witnesses during -- mentioned this family, the Zec family, a pretty wealthy family from Zagreb who is actually from Prijedor area and they were buried in Prijedor area as well, and being killed in 1991, that also had a great impact of -- on Prijedor municipality. So we thought that it's pretty important to show this incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: They were buried in Donja Dragotina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's right. That's Prijedor municipality, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In this case we agree with majority, with the objections of the OTP, not admitted into evidence. 56, admitted into evidence; 57, admitted into evidence; 58, already admitted under D89. 59, Madam Registrar we had a problem to find it, but we believe it was already admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you give me a minute to check, I will come back to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. We would also be extremely grateful if Ms. Karper could assist and see on the database whether or not this document -- the document was already admitted into evidence. So let's leave 59 open for a moment. We have to come back to this. 60, admitted into evidence; the same is true for 61 through 63; 64 is already admitted as S6; 65 through 67, admitted into evidence; 68 through 72, admitted into evidence; 73, already admitted as SK13; 74 through 80, admitted into evidence. Then once again, the same problem; we are convinced that document 81 is already admitted into evidence but we didn't find the D number. This is a Santours advertisement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. Karper has checked, and document 59 is SK40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: SK40. Thank you very much. And 81?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: She's checking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This was on late Friday afternoon when we saw this. Then 82, already admitted as S83.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 81 is D-something -- 76.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: D76. Thank you. Then 83, admitted into evidence. 84, there's no translation and the photos are not clear. So in essence we can't see the meaning of this document and this entire page. If the Defence could assist us or decide to withdraw, this would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have a translation, Your Honour, and we can provide it during the break. So maybe you can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you tell us which part of this entire document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The title of the whole page is "Picture; story from the Prijedor front." So all pictures are actually one set.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to -- sorry to say that we can't really see something on these photos, and it doesn't assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's about dugout in some village named Kahrimanovic, where Becim Mejdujanin [phoen] was hiding at that time allegedly. Photographs of Ustasha minister, Andrija Tukavis [phoen] found there, war map, if it's visible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Fortunately they are not -- we have already two copies and they are not legible. May I ask the Prosecution, what's the basis for their agreement with this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think there's any rhyme or reason to any of this, Your Honour. I think we must have worked out that it was relevant. We only object on the grounds that we think are proper, and we couldn't think of any reason to object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We can see now that a translation is available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. 85 through 87, admitted into evidence; 88 through 94, admitted into evidence; 95 through 105, admitted into evidence. 106, you will share the view of not -- non-relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This document -- this document shows that every nation in the former Yugoslavia thought about creation of new states and asked for borders to be revised, and it's one day before the referendum in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the text is issued by a Croatian National Party. So if they claim that Serbs wanted to create state inside Bosnia or to keep Bosnia inside Yugoslavia, we think that it's necessary to show that other political parties had similar views at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We could argue on the basis of tu quoque, but here we decided to state that there is no relevance for the concrete case; therefore, not admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But Judge -- Your Honour, it's not tu quoque, because it's not a crime to express political views.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... sense, but there -- I think it's undisputed that there was similar movement in other regions of the former Yugoslavia. It's not contested. So therefore, not admitted into evidence, 106. 107, 108, admitted into evidence. 109, do you have some problems?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Prosecution objected to this evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the date is the very date of the first day of referendum in Bosnia-Herzegovina and shows the example of attack on the JNA, Yugoslav National Army about roadblocks and about European Community monitors trying to solve the problem. So it shows already at that time there were problems, there were fights, and the European Community monitors involved in the whole process. So of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. 110 would be the next one. Sarajevo Radio-TV occupied. We can't see any relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Oslobodjenje paper is from Sarajevo and it mostly deals with the events from Sarajevo. So all we wanted to achieve through these articles is to show the overall situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Very few articles from Oslobodjenje deals with Prijedor area. It's Muslim-controlled papers already at that time, and we tried through Muslim-controlled papers to show from their view what the situation in Bosnia is. We didn't want to lean on any Serbian source. So having this late translation, we couldn't present those evidence to the witnesses, but we think that having the whole picture in front of us, it would be much easier to understand all the events happening in Prijedor area as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We came to the conclusion that the mere fact that Sarajevo Radio-TV was occupied was not and is not relevant for our concrete case; therefore, not admitted into evidence. 111, we have problems with the content of the document because we have before us only two pages in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is just propaganda material, so we can withdraw this document. There is nothing crucial in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: 111, withdrawn. 112, death at the barricades, 1st of March, blockade near Turbe.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, it's the second day of referendum in Bosnia, and some barricades were already in place all over the Bosnia and on one of them on the second day of referendum two men were killed, not in Prijedor area, outside Prijedor area, but we think that it shows the overall situation in Bosnia where at that time almost all roads were already blocked or unsafe to travel on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Not admitted into evidence because not related to the concrete area. 113, and a number of following documents we had a problem. If you could, please, explain where the village of Drvar is located.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 113 actually shows -- explained in the Muslim-controlled newspapers that there were irregularities, something irregular, during that referendum. And it's mentioned in this article that two men were captured with the forged papers and forged decisions. And during our case we claimed that there were some irregularities during this, the whole procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please explain where -- we were really interested in where Drvar and Bosansko Grahovo is located.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: West of Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Is it in the municipality or without?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Outside the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Outside the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Different municipalities, yes. Bordering Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Therefore, not admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry, one correction: They do not border Prijedor municipality. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Not admitted into evidence. 114?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I withdraw this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Withdrawn. 115?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Through 150, which consists of 15 various documents when they are translated but actually only three pages, I think, from the newspapers, Oslobodjenje, I just wanted to show the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina one day after the referendum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But all related to Sarajevo and Kosija Kupres [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's right. And we think that this shows complete chaos in Sarajevo at that time one day after referendum, and we think that it also shows that the referendum created a lot of problems all over Bosnia and that there were -- there was resistance all over Bosnia to its implementation and acceptance, and it's not -- that it was nothing specific for Prijedor area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As to the fact that not related to Prijedor municipality, not admitted into evidence. 116, 117, admitted into evidence. 118, new street names in Livno. We can't see the relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The names in Livno were changed -- actually, the names of the recognised people from World War II were changed into Croatian heroes from the same war, actually, who fought on the other side, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This happened in Livno; therefore, not admitted into evidence. 119?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This article deals with the propaganda through Oslobodjenje papers that was the support that was given by Oslobodjenje papers to the referendum. And obviously being read all over the Bosnia, this propaganda had impact on Prijedor area as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG

There should be evidence if that's what the purpose is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We believe that we have to be fair and consequent we asked counsel to confer with the client whether or not it would be the submission that this document would be signed by Dr. Stakic in person, and now it's only consequent when he states that it's in fact not the signature that we admit these documents into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, may I just make one small point on this. We can, if necessary, call evidence to show that in the Brdjanin case, Brdjanin in a document that he was obliged to sign for the court deliberately signed in a way that was not his normal signature. Your Honour, it is in our submission quite wrong and negates any idea why an accused gives evidence that it is sufficient in this court for an accused to give instructions to say it's not my signature and for that to be taken as evidence of that fact. It's not evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The burden of proof is with the Prosecution. The Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But we didn't put the document in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: That's right. You put -- you have put a number of documents from a number of periods of time in, and we accepted this and we accept now this document with the additional explanation by Defence counsel. I think we shouldn't go in further detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just one thing, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These documents are signed in 1992 or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It reads 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 1995, not recently. So it's not done purposefully and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So we take into account the document with the additional explanation by counsel. 579 was already admitted under D120; 580 was already admitted under D121; 581, already admitted under D122; 582, already admitted under D123. Then we come to the question of document 583. And here -- it's a document signed by a liaison officer, and the content would be, Mr. Lukic? Because we don't have any English version of this. Do we have it already on the transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's been read out already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If you could just repeat what it states. To the best of my recollection, it was a -- please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's from Ministry of Justice from RS, from bureau -- liaison actually bureau with the International Tribunal in Den Haag. I will read in B/C/S so you can receive the proper translation. [Interpretation] "Regarding your enactment number 02/1-773-31/02, concerning your request by the enactment of the general staff of the Republika Srpska army, internal number 03/2155-2, dated 12 February 2002, we hereby inform you of the following: We quote, `We hereby inform you that the appointment of military commanders and their deputies in military units which were stationed in Prijedor municipality during the period from 1991 to 1992 was dealt with according to the chain of management and command in the army. Here above indicates that Mr. Milomir Stakic as the president of the Municipal Assembly and the Crisis Staff of Prijedor municipality during the aforementioned period could not have influenced the appointment and nomination of military commanders and their deputies.' Liaison Officer Zoran Cvetkovic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This was the document I mentioned yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And for your information, Your Honour, it was Ms. Sutherland who dealt with it, and neither myself or Mr. Koumjian, so I hope Your Honour will forgive both myself and Mr. Koumjian, not knowing what you were talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, may I just read what you're stating. My sincere apologies. But let's come to the subject matter of the question before us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's objectionable. It's objectionable because this man doesn't know, is a liaison officer, is in no position to give this information. It's a hotly disputed issue in this case. And the right thing to do would have been to call him and subject him to cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I take the liberty to state that it was just that what I stated yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Knowing what we decided in regard with the statement of Ms. Biljana Plavsic, we withdraw this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. 584 was already decided as not admitted; 585 was withdrawn. So this would mean that we would be able now to come to the second reading. We have to come back to document 309. A translation was missing. Then for document 2, the Defence mentioned that we would get the copy of the whole book only later, and then it was a question of the five chapters of book number 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Ms. Korner, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour said you only required one copy of the chapters of the Halilovic book, so that's what we provided. No doubt your legal officers can have a lot of fun reading it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I hope that you are -- agree that also the Judges have the right to read it. Yes? Anything else missing, may I ask, Madam Registrar, on the list of missing documents or other documents with problems?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. For the record, I was asked to confirm that number 328 is indeed S341. I double-checked. And number 330 is S345. We still have to rule on the admission of D55. We admitted the report by Mr. Corin relating to those two -- to the statute, but the actual statute of which we have two different copies needs to be dealt with. And for S430, we need a final translation from the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, on the last, I'm told that was submitted yesterday. Sorry. It was submitted for translation yesterday. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So when could we receive the final translation of S430?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We'll have to speak to the CLSS about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When you mentioned the report by Mr. Corin, it was J33? Because on the transcript it reads D55.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This report pertains to the Exhibit number D55, which has not been admitted because we had the first excerpt submitted by the Defence and then the OTP provided a copy of the whole statute and the two documents presented discrepancies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we already came to the decision that we should admit both copies because they are different. The one with one -- with the cover page "Statute," and the P number 0020412 would be D55, and the other one, the other copy of the same document, would be D55-1.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, D55 was seized from the municipal assembly building in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we also have a translation for the Defence, number -- the document number 302.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Anything else on problematic documents?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Are there any other issues to be discussed, any other --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence Exhibit 566, although it was submitted by the team that deals with the Kosovo matters, and that's why it's got the K number, it does not necessarily mean that it's a Kosovo document, but it is from the document to do with the JNA in general. That's all we can say. Your Honour, the only other issue that I wish to raise is what Your Honour mentioned this morning, and that is Dr. Stakic having the last word. And you won't be surprised in the light of what I've just objected to. Your Honour was saying this, we don't imagine it will carry much weight. But the Rules don't allow for Dr. Stakic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't want to repeat this. Ms. Korner, we have stated this since the beginning of the case. And to be honest, slowly I am losing my patience. What you stated just a minute before, this was unheard. There were so many statements given in writing by members of the Prosecution on evidently -- evidently false submissions, and I had to do the necessary to prove the contrary, and there was no one apology through -- throughout the entire year. And I will not allow that in a courtroom where I preside a Prosecutor denies the right of an accused to have the last word, and this is my last word on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I understand that. But Your Honour, for the reasons that Your Honour is aware of, I wish to make it clear there's an objection to which Your Honour has overruled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You know that there is already a case, the case of Kunarac appeal, where the Appeals Chamber decided to grant the last word as a human right. And if you want to deny human rights of an accused, then you are wrong in this room.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Your Honour, I want the Rules of Evidence to be complied with that are part of this court. That is what I want.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: There are higher rights, higher-ranking rights than our fragmentary Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and those are human rights, and you should be aware of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am well aware, as Your Honour is, of human rights. There are rules which are designed for trials at this court. If Your Honour wishes to have those rules changed, then of course Your Honour is in a position to do so. But those are the rules, and they are not being complied with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, do you want to make the statement that the Appeals Chamber presided over by the President of this Tribunal ruled and decided against the law?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Decided against the Rules of Procedure and Evidence deliberately?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Is this your statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I am saying is that situation was a different situation which pertains in this court now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: My statement is a final one. It is unheard that in a court, in a tribunal, tailor-made and designed to protect human rights, the Office of the Prosecutor by senior legal officer denies human rights of the accused.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is an outrageous suggestion. I am not, by the way, a senior legal officer. I am a senior trial attorney. It is an outrage to suggest that. But as Your Honour knows, I have throughout this case been concerned with the fact that the rules laid down by the Judges of this Tribunal are not being followed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You had already once made the experience that the Appeals Chamber had to decide that your submissions were frivolous ones. You can repeat this. Are there any other real issues to be discussed?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then let's come back to the calendar in order that we have all the possibilities exhausted related to the courtrooms we need and, on the other hand, to give place for other cases to be heard. I think we came to the conclusion that the closing arguments by the Prosecution would be given on Friday, the 11th of April. Therefore, we would not need a courtroom until this day. The closing arguments given by the Defence would follow, the 14th of April, Monday. The response to this, the 15th; the response to this and the last word, the 16th of April. And let us, please, make, if need may be, for maybe additional questions the 17th of April, that is, Thursday. So we would need the entire week from 14th to 17th. Friday would be a holiday. And then for the purpose of a final brief, of course we don't know -- we don't need any courtroom. And then we have to decide and find out when a judgment can be ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I can't see that anybody else wants to take the floor; therefore, I declare today's hearing closed. And the trial stays adjourned until we hear the closing remarks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
